newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: BRYANT GETS CHANCE TO EXPLAIN
Port Arthur gunman, Martin Bryant, will get the chance today to tell his side of the story.
The opportunity will come at the end of the Crown case against the 29-year-old Hobart man, who's pleaded guilty to 72 charges, including 35 of murder.
Today, the court will hear a two-hour videotape of a police interview with Bryant, who the prosecution says has never given any reason for his actions.
The court will hear details of Bryant's background, and a victim impact statement will be read.
Defence counsel, John Avery, may then enter a plea in mitigation, and tender medical reports.
Mr Avery says he won't know until later today what his instructions will be.
US President off to National Capital
US President Bill Clinton will head to the Nation's capital this morning to meet with Prime Minister John Howard and address Federal Parliament.
The President and his wife Hillary arrived in Sydney slightly behind schedule last night after a delayed take-off from Honolulu.

His talks with John Howard are expected to centre on trade and the Asia Pacific, and after addressing the joint sitting of parliament, the President will return to Sydney for an evening harbour cruise.
Bill Clinton is the third President to visit Australia, following in the footsteps of his predecessor George Bush five years ago, and Lyndon Johnson in the sixties.
IR LEGISLATION GETS THROUGH PARLIAMENT
The Government has described last night's passing of the first piece of its industrial relations legislation as a giant step in advancing Australian living standards.
Federal Industrial Relations minister Peter Reith says the new system will deliver real benefits to workers and businesses, encourage job creation, and protect the disadvantaged.
The Coalition got the legislation through Parliament after months of negotiations with the Australian Democrats.
During the sitting, Opposition and Greens Senators continued until to put up amendments, including those to protect workers' bargaining powers, unions, the I-R-C, and awards, but most were rejected.
The Government says it's new industrial relations system will start operating in the New Year.
LISTING OIL RIG TO BE SAVED ASAP
A Danish company which owns the oil rig listing in Gulf St Vincent, near Adelaide, plans to recover it as soon as possible. This follows underwater and aerial inspections of the rig.
Its legs have to be retracted or removed, before it can be put back on a heavy-lift ship, which brought it from the North West Shelf.
Texas-based Canyon, which plans to lease the rig from its Danish owners, says it will probably be taken to Singapore for repair.
BETTER TIMES AHEAD FOR COLES MYER
Shareholders of retailing giant, Coles Myer, slammed the company's board at its annual general meeting yesterday.
Criticisms centred on a slump in profits, a big pay rise for the firm's chief executive, and the handling of the so-called "Yannon transaction".
Coles Myer Chairman, Nobby Clark, has admitted the company's performance has been abysmal, but he's looking forward to better times.
Mr Clark says there's nothing wrong with Coles-Myer that three or four half years of good bottomline performance won't cure.
He says much has been done by the retailer behind the scenes, and the benefits of this work should begin to come through in this financial year, if the Christmas shopping period is reasonable.
SAFE SEX SERMON STARTS SUNDAY
The benefits of safe sex are to be brought home to Australians during AIDS awareness week, which starts on Sunday.
AIDS Council President, Noel Hobson, says the week, which incorporates world AIDS Day, will also extol the virtues of greater tolerance by all.
In the next 12 months more than three million people worldwide will contract HIV or AIDS this year, translating to five infections every minute.
Mr Hobson says AIDS awareness week is one way of trying to combat the spread of the virus.
BACKPACKER VISA RELAXATION REQUIRED
Tourism operators are to warn the Federal Government restrictions on work visas are keeping backpackers from coming to Australia.
A conference in Sydney will this morning hear the backpacker market is continuing to grow, and is increasing in importance, especially in regional areas.
Tourism Council Executive Director, Bruce Baird, says the new restrictions mean that as soon as budget travellers settle into Australian jobs, they have to leave.
Mr Baird says the Government will come under pressure from the industry to relax the rules.
JACKSON HEADS TO MELBOURNE
Rock star Michael Jackson will be greeted by a troop of aborignal dancers when he arrives at his Melbourne Hotel this afternoon.
Continuing on his National HIStory tour, Jackson will be also be treated to the release of white doves and a performance by the National boys choir.
Students from the Victorian School of the Deaf will also sing the singer's "Heal the World" song.
Jackson will perform two shows at the M-C-G on Friday and Sunday.
